Approach

A theory counts as most accurate only if it explains the known facts and predicts data it never saw

No theory has done this yet. The same rules as our Indus script project: a good-looking result must not be able to come from trying until something works.

The goalFive rulesTrapsLevelOur own theoryNot claimed

01Goal

“Most accurate” means all eight of these tests are passed

“Most accurate” has to be checkable. A theory, ours or anyone's, wins only if it explains the established facts best and predicts new data better than its rivals. All of these must hold:

  1. Written down and frozen. The theory states what brain activity comes with experience, and why. Its measure and decision rule are hashed before any held-out data is opened.
  2. Explains the known facts. It accounts for more of our public list of established findings than any rival does (blindsight, split brains, the cerebellum, anaesthesia, dreaming, covert awareness and more), scored by people who did not write it.
  3. Works zero-shot. It tells conscious from unconscious on at least 4 held-out datasets from 3 families (sleep, anaesthesia, disorders of consciousness), with AUC at least 0.90 pooled and 0.80 in each.
  4. Right when behaviour misleads. Ketamine (unresponsive, but people report experiences afterwards), REM dreaming, and dream vs no-dream awakenings within one sleep stage. The truth is the later report.
  5. Beats simple baselines. It outperforms the EEG spectral slope, band power and an arousal classifier. Otherwise it is a sleepiness detector.
  6. Beats rival theories. At least two rival measures, frozen the same way, score worse.
  7. Prospective. It passes on a dataset published after the hash date.
  8. Survives a red team that did not build it.

What would raise the odds most

  • An open TMS-EEG dataset covering sleep, anaesthesia and patients, so the perturbational complexity index can be tested directly.
  • Open, pooled dream reports from serial-awakening studies.
  • COGITATE experiment 2 or INTREPID data released after we seal our predictions, which would give a clean prospective test.

02Rules

Five rules stop a good-looking result from fooling us

  1. Seal it before you look.Each measure, its preprocessing, its threshold and its pass mark are written down and SHA-256 hashed before we see any outcome.
  2. Test on people it never saw.Data is split by subject, and data from the same lab counts as a near-copy when we test transfer.
  3. Plant an answer first.A pipeline must recover an injected effect of known size, and must not call spectrum-matched noise 'conscious', before its output on real data counts.
  4. Let someone else try to break it.Every positive result goes to a red team that did not produce it.
  5. Publish it either way.Failed routes are written up with the size of effect the test could have caught.

03Traps

Most measures can be fooled by sleepiness, small samples or flexible analysis

  • Report is the only ground truth. Every label is inferred from someone's report or behaviour, so we grade each label by what it rests on.
  • Unresponsive is not unconscious. Ketamine and dreaming show the gap, which is why they are our hardest tests.
  • The spectrum hides everything. Many complexity measures move with slow-wave power; we compare every measure against it.
  • Analytic flexibility. The same COGITATE data has already been read both ways on offset ignition.
  • Small samples. Most open datasets have 10-30 people; every negative states what it could have detected.

04Level

We name the level of every claim, and test which level carries the state

Theories of consciousness disagree about scale: single neurons, local loops, brain areas or the whole brain. A test at the wrong scale can miss a real effect or find a fake one. Findings explains why the level matters.

  • Our data sets the level we can test. Scalp EEG adds up the activity of millions of neurons over centimetres and milliseconds. Our tests can support or rule out claims at that scale. A claim about single neurons or molecules is marked silent on our data, not contradicted.
  • Every prediction names its level. Each sealed plan states the spatial scale (one channel, a group of channels, the whole head) and the time window it is about. A result is only reported at that scale.
  • We test which level carries the state. Planned: predict reported experience from the same awakenings at several grains, from single channels to the whole head and from 1 to 30 seconds, held out by person and lab. If a coarser grain predicts better than its parts, that is evidence the state lives at that level. The Rosas and Mediano measure is a second check. First, the method must find the right level in data built so that only one level carries the answer.
  • Our own theory must say its level. A draft theory that does not say at which scale its mechanism works cannot make risky predictions, so it cannot pass step four of the build.

05Build

Testing theories only shows which fail, so we are also building one

Any theory, ours included, is scored by agents who did not write it, may not be revised after its predictions are opened without a new hash and a new test, and goes into the list of closed routes if it fails.

06Not claimed

Even a winning theory would not explain why experience exists

  • The hard problem. A theory that predicts exactly which brain activity comes with experience would still not say why there is experience at all. We say so on every page.
  • AI sentience. We use AI systems only to stress-test theories, and never treat a model's self-report as evidence.
  • Clinical use. A measure that does well here is not a diagnostic for patients.

Goal: find the most accurate theory of human consciousness, by 2027.

An open research project run by a human lead and a team of AI agents. Every result can be rerun from code.
